nedenunder.explanation: "Nedenunder" means "downstairs". It is built from "neden" (below) and "under" (under). To say a room is on the floor above instead, use "ovenpå" (upstairs): "Soveværelset er ovenpå" (The bedroom is upstairs).

nedslående.explanation: "Nedslående" means "disheartening". To describe bad news, use it before the noun: "nedslående nyheder" (disheartening news). To say a person feels low, use "nedtrykt" (downcast): "Hun er nedtrykt" (She is downcast).

nedtrykt.explanation: "Nedtrykt" means "downcast". It is built from "ned" (down) and "trykt" (pressed), so it literally means "pressed down". To say someone seems low in spirit, say: "Hun virker nedtrykt i dag" (She seems downcast today).

negativ.explanation: "Negativ" means "negative". To say a medical test found nothing, use it for the result: "Testen var negativ" (The test was negative).

neglelak.explanation: "Neglelak" means "nail polish". It is built from "negle" (nails) and "en lak" (a lacquer). To take it off, you need "neglelakfjerner" (nail polish remover): "Har du neglelakfjerner?" (Do you have nail polish remover?)

nej.explanation: "Nej" means "no". When you are surprised or impressed, it also means "oh!": "Nej, hvor er det flot!" (Oh, how beautiful!) To answer yes to a question with "ikke" (not), say "jo" (yes) instead of "ja": "Kan du ikke komme?" "Jo, det kan jeg." (Can't you come? Yes, I can.)

nem.explanation: "Nem" means "easy". To say something is easy to do, use "nem at" (easy to) before the verb: "Appen er nem at bruge" (The app is easy to use). To say a task is hard instead, use "svær" (hard): "en svær opgave" (a hard task).

nemlig.explanation: "Nemlig" means "exactly". To agree with someone, say it as a reply: "Er du træt?" "Nemlig!" (Are you tired? Exactly!) When you give a reason inside a sentence, it means "you see": "Jeg bliver hjemme, jeg er nemlig syg" (I am staying home, I am sick, you see).

nemt.explanation: "Nemt" means "easy". To say how something is done, it means "easily": "Han vinder nemt" (He wins easily). With an "en" word, use "nem" instead: "en nem opgave" (an easy task).

nervepirrende.explanation: "Nervepirrende" means "nerve-wracking". It is built from "en nerve" (a nerve) and "pirrende" (irritating). To describe a movie that makes you tense, say: "en nervepirrende film" (a nerve-wracking movie).

nervøs.explanation: "Nervøs" means "nervous". To say you feel it before something important, say: "Jeg er nervøs før eksamen" (I am nervous before the exam). To say someone is calm instead, use "rolig" (calm): "Hun er helt rolig" (She is completely calm).

nervøsitet.explanation: "En nervøsitet" means "a nervousness". It comes from "nervøs" (nervous). The ending "-itet" is also in "en aktivitet" (an activity). To say someone showed none, say: "Han viste ingen nervøsitet" (He showed no nervousness).

netop.explanation: "Netop" means "exactly". To agree with exactly what someone said, say it as a reply: "Netop!" (Exactly!) To say something happened a moment ago, it means "just": "Han er netop gået" (He just left).

neutral.explanation: "Neutral" means "neutral". To say a country takes no side in a conflict, say: "et neutralt land" (a neutral country). To say a color goes with everything, such as gray, say: "en neutral farve" (a neutral color).

ni.explanation: "Ni" means "nine". The same "ni" starts "nitten" (nineteen) and "niende" (ninth). To say a multiplication, say: "Tre gange ni er syvogtyve" (Three times nine is twenty-seven).

niende.explanation: "Niende" means "ninth". To put things in order, use it after "den" (the): "den niende dag" (the ninth day). To say a date, use it before the month: "den niende maj" (the ninth of May).

nitten.explanation: "Nitten" means "nineteen". To say how much money you have, say: "Jeg har nitten kroner" (I have nineteen kroner).

nogen.explanation: "Nogen" means "anyone". To say you see a person, it means "someone": "Jeg ser nogen" (I see someone). In a question, or after "ikke" (not), it also means "any": "Har du nogen børn?" (Do you have any children?)

nogenlunde.explanation: "Nogenlunde" means "reasonably". To answer "How is it going?" with "so-so", say it as a reply: "Hvordan går det?" "Nogenlunde." (How is it going? So-so.)

nogensinde.explanation: "Nogensinde" means "ever". To ask about your whole life, use it in a question: "Har du nogensinde været i Paris?" (Have you ever been to Paris?) To say never, use "aldrig" (never): "Jeg har aldrig været i Paris" (I have never been to Paris).

noget.explanation: "Noget" means "something". To say you see a thing, say: "Jeg ser noget" (I see something). To say you see a person, use "nogen" (someone): "Jeg ser nogen" (I see someone). Before something you cannot count one by one, such as milk, it means "some": "noget mælk" (some milk).

nogle.explanation: "Nogle" means "some", and it goes with more than one thing: "Jeg har nogle venner" (I have some friends). To talk about one thing, use "en" (a): "Jeg har en ven" (I have one friend). In a question, or after "ikke" (not), use "nogen" (any): "Har du nogen venner?" (Do you have any friends?)

nogle gange.explanation: "Nogle gange" means "sometimes" (literally, "some times"). To say you do something now and then, put it in the sentence: "Jeg spiser nogle gange morgenmad" (I sometimes eat breakfast). To say always, use "altid" (always): "Jeg spiser altid morgenmad" (I always eat breakfast).

nok.explanation: "Nok" means "enough". To say you have enough of something, say: "Jeg har nok mad" (I have enough food). To say what you guess will happen, it means "probably": "Han kommer nok" (He will probably come).

nord.explanation: "Nord" means "north". To say where something is, use "i nord" (in the north): "Skoven ligger i nord" (The forest is in the north). To say which way you are going, use "mod nord" (toward the north): "Vi kører mod nord" (We drive toward the north). The same "nord" is in "Nordjylland" (North Jutland).
